title: AI is everywhere except in the GDP numbers — here is what triggers the break
description: The productivity data doesn't show the AI boom, and won't until companies stop cost-cutting and start building. Nobody is positioning for that trade.
content: About a year and a half ago, I was invited to an event abroad with some extremely well-known founders from around the world. Three days of conversations about technology and everything technology touches. It was great. Recommended Video During one of the AI breakouts, a group of us started comparing notes. Most of the people in the room had known Collective[i] for years. Some as customers. Some as investors. Some as friendly skeptics who had watched us build something that did not fit the standard tech narrative until AI became the thing. Now we were at the start of the AI mass revolution, and everyone had questions. The scale of what we had been building, the speed of adoption, and the revenue growth were finally large enough that the skeptics were the ones asking how to participate. Here is the thing about that room. Every one of them had missed AI at the front end. Every great VC and every great founder had. In tech circles, if you miss a revolution you are not in the know, so you fake it, hard, and you look for a way to have been involved early. Andreessen Horowitz ‘s participation in the recent OpenAI rounds is a good example. Those rounds were priced at $150 billion in late 2024, then $300 billion in March 2025, then $852 billion in March 2026. That is late-stage private equity written on venture letterhead. I am not sure any of it counts as venture anymore. The room was full of that energy. Everyone talking about how great AI was, and how fast it was going to change the world. I asked one question. If AI is what everyone in this room just said it is, why are we not seeing a drop in inflation? Why is GDP growth not spiking? Where is any of this in the numbers? They looked at me like I was a traitor. Every person in that room was calling themselves an AI person by then, and every one of them nervously laughed when I asked. If you had been late to the party, cheerleading was the safest posture. Any hint of skepticism read like evidence you had been on the wrong side of the biggest shift in a decade. I had been building on what people now call AI for ten years at Collective[i], so I did not care how the question landed. I asked it anyway. I think it is the exact question everyone should be asking. How fast the benefits of a truly life-changing technology flow through the economy is the actual measure of how fast it is being adopted. What the Collective[i] network sees says the answer is faster than almost anyone expects. Across the enterprises inside the network, we watch companies pick the wrong people, run the wrong approach, and still see the fixes land in weeks instead of years. I have written elsewhere on this blog, in The Trade-Off Nobody Is Making , about the millions of people who now have access to a doctor, a lawyer, or a tutor through a large language model who never had access to any of those before. That is a life-changing shift for a large share of the world’s population, and it happened in twenty-four months. The question that got laughed at is not a new one either. In July 1987, the economist Robert Solow wrote one of the most quoted lines in the history of macroeconomics. “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” It took another decade of computer investment before US productivity growth actually broke out of its long stall. The data did not show what everyone knew was happening. We are living inside the same paradox now. AI is in every earnings call. It is in every board deck. It is in every job ad, every product roadmap, every consulting pitch. Enterprise spend on generative AI ran to $30 to $40 billion in 2025 alone. The productivity statistics show almost nothing. One exception is worth naming. Data center construction is booming, and that capex shows up in GDP as private nonresidential fixed investment. It is meaningful to the headline number. In 2025 the hyperscalers alone poured more than $300 billion into data centers, chips, and grid capacity, and that spend is doing real work in the top-line growth figures. Strip it out and the underlying growth picture is even flatter than the headline suggests. The right question is not why. The right question is when it changes. Because it does change. The trigger is measurable if you know what to watch for. My prior piece, The Trillion-Dollar Trade Wall Street Isn’t Seeing , argued that every adoption curve is getting shorter than the last. The AI break-out is not going to take the fifteen years computers took to show up in the productivity data. It is going to take five to eight, for the reasons I laid out there. That compression is what makes the phase three moment tradable inside every current fund horizon. This piece is the case for the trigger, and for the trade that sits underneath it. Phase One. Everyone Just Caught Up on the Backlog. Across the Collective[i] network, we shipped more product in the first six months of 2026 than in the previous two years combined. That is a meaningful jump. It should feel like an advantage. Except that unless you are living under a tree, so has everyone else. The speed of software development jumped for every company at roughly the same time, which is exactly why it created no meaningful advantage for any of them. Every team had an endless backlog of features, integrations, edge cases, and quality improvements they had been putting off for years. AI-assisted development, agent workflows, and vibe coding all landed at once. The backlogs are getting worked down. That is a real gift to the users of these products. It is not new revenue for anyone building them. The same pattern shows up in almost every function. It takes less time to write a marketing report. So leaders ask for more content in the reports. It takes less time to build a customer segmentation. So the segmentation gets rerun weekly instead of quarterly. It takes less time to draft a legal review. So legal reviews five more contracts a week. The output scales up. The bill for producing it goes down. GDP measures neither of those things very well, because national accounts were designed to count units of sale and hours worked, not the quality or richness of what got produced. Net-net, this is a genuine improvement for the customers of everything. It is not a growth signal. Phase Two. Cost Cutting Is the Default First Move. The second phase looks the same as the first from ten thousand feet. Companies deploy AI. The stock analysts hear about it. Nothing shows up in the topline. The difference is where the money goes. Agents are enabling more work to be done by fewer people, and almost every enterprise deploying them is aiming that saving at cost, not at growth. Why pay a CRM vendor when a small team can build a working version over a weekend in Claude . Why staff a Tier-1 customer support desk when an agent can resolve the same tickets at a quarter of the cost. Why pay for BPO contracts when internal automation handles the same volume. Cost savings is the default first move for almost every leader. I have made this case in every piece I have written on the AI-first transition. In The Companies Winning at AI Are Playing a Different Game , I argued the winners rebuild. In What It Means to Be AI-First , I gave the operational playbook. In The Safest Move You Can Make With AI , I explained why the cautious position is the expensive one. The pattern is consistent. Most companies are in cost-cutting mode. A small minority is building something new. The evidence is not soft. MIT’s Project NANDA studied more than 300 enterprise AI deployments in 2025 and found 95% delivered zero measurable P&L impact. The other 5% is where the real money is being made. That distribution is not a temporary phenomenon. It is the standard shape of a General Purpose Technology transition.
